decks.title: What a Constructor Is: Default and Parameterised Constructors
goals: State the characteristics of a constructor and when it is executed
Explain the default constructor supplied by the compiler and when it is not supplied
Write a class with a default and a parameterised constructor to initialise data members
Use the keyword this when parameters have the names of data members

slides.heading: Constructors
slides.body_md: Part 1: what a **constructor** is, its **characteristics**, **object creation**, the **default constructor**, the **parameterised constructor** and the keyword **this**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what a constructor is, its characteristics, object creation, the default constructor, the parameterised constructor and the keyword this with common mistakes
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to the chapter on constructors. In this first part we learn what a constructor is, how it is written, and exactly when it runs. We study the default constructor that the compiler supplies, and the parameterised constructor that takes the starting values. Then we meet the keyword this, and the common mistakes that the compiler reports with real error messages.

slides.heading: What is a constructor?
slides.body_md: A **constructor** is a member method of a class that is executed **automatically** when an object is created, to **initialise the data members** of the object.

rows: the same as the class name, letter for letter
none at all, not even void
automatically by new, once for each object
gives the data members their starting values

visual.alt: Table of the four features of a constructor: it has the class name, has no return type, is executed automatically by new once for each object, and is used to give the data members starting values

slides.narration: A constructor is a special member method of a class. It runs automatically when an object is created, and its job is to give the data members their starting values. The table lists four features. It has the same name as the class. It has no return type, not even void. It is run by the new operator, once for each object. And it is used to initialise data members.

slides.heading: The first constructor

rows: the object is created and the default constructor runs
the method prints the two data members

visual.alt: Table tracing the Parcel program: the creation prints Parcel created and show then prints 500 g, Rs 35.0
visual.caption: The constructor prints before any method is called.

slides.narration: Here is our first constructor, in a class for a courier parcel. It has the class name, no return type, and it sets the weight and the charge. It also prints a message. When the statement creating the object is executed, the message appears at once, before any method is called. Then the show method prints the two data members.

slides.body_md: Follow the statement `Parcel p = new Parcel();` step by step.

visual.caption: The variable p holds a reference; the data members live in the object.

slides.narration: Let us see what the creation statement builds. The variable p is only a reference. The new operator makes an object, and the constructor stores the weight five hundred and the charge thirty five in its data members. The reference p then points to that object. The reference lives in p, but the data members live in the object.

slides.narration: Decide which statements run a constructor, and which only look as if they do.

slides.heading: What does new do?
slides.body_md: The constructor does not create the object. It runs **after** the memory is allocated, and the data members already hold their **default values** when its body starts.

nodes.label: Memory is allocated for the object

visual.alt: Flow of object creation: new is executed, memory is allocated, data members get default values, the constructor body runs and the reference is stored in the variable
visual.caption: What new does, step by step

slides.narration: This flow shows the steps of object creation. First new is executed. Memory is allocated for the object, and the data members receive their default values. Only then does the body of the constructor run and assign the starting values. At the end, the reference to the finished object is stored in the variable. So a constructor initialises an object, but it is the new operator that creates it.

slides.heading: Data members without a constructor

visual.alt: Table of default values of data members in a class with no constructor: an int is 0, a double is 0.0, a boolean is false and a String is null
visual.caption: The class Kiosk has no constructor and no assignment.

slides.narration: If no statement gives a data member a value, Java supplies the default value of its type. An int is zero, a double is zero point zero, a boolean is false, and a String, like every object, is null. Notice that this class has no constructor, yet the object is created without any error. The next slide explains why.

slides.heading: Quick check: default values
slides.body_md: Write the exact output.
slides.narration: Remember the default value of each type: number, boolean and object.

slides.heading: The default constructor
slides.body_md: If a class has **no constructor**, the compiler supplies a **default constructor** with no parameters. If the class has **any** constructor, the compiler supplies nothing.

rows: works: count is 2 after two calls of sell()
compile-time error: constructor Parcel in class Parcel cannot be applied to given types;

visual.alt: Table of the compiler-supplied default constructor: a class with no constructor works with new and its count reaches 2 after two calls; a class with only a parameterised constructor gives the compile-time error constructor Parcel in class Parcel cannot be applied to given types;
visual.caption: The default constructor is supplied only to a class that has none of its own.

slides.narration: Why can an object of a class without constructors be created? The compiler supplies a default constructor, with no parameters, to any class that has none. But the moment the programmer writes any constructor, even one with a parameter, the compiler stops supplying it. Then a creation with no arguments fails, and the table shows the real compiler message.

slides.heading: Parameterised constructors

visual.alt: Trace table of the parameterised constructor of Rickshaw: the call with 3 and 12.5 and a trip of 8 km prints 3 100.0; the call with 4 and 9.5 and a trip of 6 km prints 4 57.0
visual.caption: Arguments reach the parameters in the order they are written.

slides.narration: A parameterised constructor receives the starting values as arguments. In the rickshaw class the constructor has two parameters, the seats and the fare per kilometre. The arguments are passed in order, so three goes to seats and twelve point five to the fare. Different objects can now start with different values, as the two rows of the table show.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: tracing a parameterised constructor

visual.alt: Trace table of the parameterised constructor of Rickshaw: the call with 3 and 12.5 and a trip of 8 km prints 3 100.0; the call with 4 and 9.5 and a trip of 6 km prints 4 57.0
visual.caption: Arguments reach the parameters in the order they are written.

slides.narration: Let us trace a booking for four seats at nine point five rupees a kilometre, for a trip of six kilometres. The constructor stores four in seats and nine point five in the fare per kilometre. The method fare multiplies nine point five by six and returns fifty seven point zero, a double. The program prints the seats, a space, and then the fare.

slides.heading: Parameter names and this
slides.body_md: When a parameter has the **same name** as a data member, the parameter hides it. The keyword **this** refers to the **current object**: `this.name` is the data member.

rows: this used for the data members
this for name, a different parameter name for age

visual.alt: Table of the keyword this: without this the object shows null 0; with this the object shows Kavya 15; a different parameter name needs no this and also shows Kavya 15
visual.caption: name = name; assigns the parameter to itself.

slides.narration: Programmers like to give the parameters the same names as the data members. But then the simple name means the parameter. The statement name equals name assigns the parameter to itself, and the data member keeps its default, so the object shows null and zero. Writing this dot name makes the data member receive the value. A different parameter name needs no this.

slides.heading: Quick check: the missing this
slides.body_md: Write the exact output.
slides.narration: Ask which name, the parameter or the data member, each statement assigns.

slides.heading: A constructor may contain any statements

visual.alt: Trace table of the Sack constructor: the argument minus 5 makes the condition true and kg 0; the argument 40 makes it false and kg 40; the program prints 0 40
visual.caption: Any statement may be written inside a constructor.

slides.narration: A constructor is not limited to simple assignments. It may contain decisions, loops, or calls to other methods. In this class a negative weight is not accepted. The condition is true for minus five, so the weight is set to zero. For forty the condition is false, and forty is stored. The program prints zero and forty.

slides.heading: Mistake: void before the name
slides.body_md: Writing **void** before the name turns the member into an ordinary **method**. It compiles, but `new` never calls it.

headers: Output of `Diya d = new Diya(); System.out.println(d.lit);`
rows: an ordinary method that only has the class name

visual.alt: Table comparing a real constructor, which prints Diya ready / 5, with a method that has void before the class name, which prints only 0 because new does not call it
visual.caption: With void, nothing is executed by new.

slides.narration: A very common mistake is to write void before the constructor name. The compiler does not complain, because a method may share the name of its class. But it is now an ordinary method, and the new operator does not call it. The data members keep their default values, and the message never appears. The correct constructor, without void, prints Diya ready and sets lit to five.

slides.heading: Other mistakes the compiler catches
slides.body_md: A constructor has **no return type**, cannot be **static**, and is **never called** like a method.

rows: invalid method declaration; return type required

visual.alt: Table of five mistakes with constructors and the real compiler messages: invalid method declaration; return type required; incompatible types: unexpected return value; modifier static not allowed here; cannot find symbol; cannot find symbol
visual.caption: The messages are those of javac in JDK 21.

slides.narration: The table lists other mistakes with their real compiler messages. A constructor whose name differs from the class is read as a method with no return type. A constructor cannot return a value. It cannot be static. It cannot be called through the object afterwards. And the new operator must never be left out when an object is created.

slides.heading: Quick check: declaration or creation?
slides.body_md: True or false?
slides.narration: Think about whether a declaration creates an object, and what runs when it does.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: class name, no return type (not even void), run by new once per object
Parcel p; creates no object and runs no constructor
supplied by the compiler only if the class has no constructor
receives the starting values as arguments
the current object; this.name is the data member hidden by a parameter
an ordinary method that new never calls

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the rules of a constructor, its use, the declaration against creation, the default constructor, the parameterised constructor, the keyword this and the effect of void

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. A constructor has the class name and no return type, and the new operator runs it once for each object. Its use is to initialise the data members. A declaration alone runs no constructor. The compiler supplies a default constructor only if the class has none. A parameterised constructor takes starting values. The keyword this reaches a hidden data member, and void before the name makes a method.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Say all three facts about a constructor: class name, no return type (not even `void`), run by `new`.
A declaration such as `Parcel p;` creates no object: no constructor runs.
If the class has only a parameterised constructor, `new Parcel()` is a compile-time error.
In a parameterised constructor with parameters named like the data members, write `this.name = name;`.
In a program, create an object with `new` and then call its methods: constructors are never called by name.
slides.narration: Some exam tips. State the three facts about a constructor: the class name, no return type, and execution by new. Remember that a declaration alone runs nothing. A class with only a parameterised constructor cannot be created with no arguments. Use this when parameters and data members share names. And never call a constructor by its name through an object.

decks.title: Constructor Overloading and Constructors against Methods
goals: Write overloaded constructors that differ in the number, types or order of parameters
Predict which constructor is called for a given argument list, including type promotion
Trace the order of constructor messages when objects are created
Tabulate the differences between a constructor and a method

slides.heading: Constructor overloading
slides.body_md: Part 2: **constructor overloading**, **which constructor runs**, **type promotion**, **errors in calls**, **copying an object** and **constructors against methods**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: why constructors are overloaded, rules for overloading, which constructor runs, type promotion, errors in calls, copying an object and constructor against method
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to the second part. A class may have more than one constructor, and this is called constructor overloading. We learn the rules, and how Java decides which constructor runs, including what happens when the argument type does not match exactly. We trace the order of constructor messages, copy values from another object, and finish by comparing constructors with methods.

slides.heading: Why overload a constructor?
slides.body_md: Objects are not always created with the same information. **Overloaded constructors** let a class offer several ways of creating an object, each with its own parameter list.

visual.alt: Table of four overloaded constructors of the class Meter: no parameter, one int, one double and one String, each printing its own label
visual.caption: Four constructors, one class name, four different parameter lists.

slides.narration: Sometimes we know nothing about the object when we create it, sometimes one value, sometimes several. Constructor overloading allows several constructors in one class, all with the class name. The class in the table has four constructors, with no parameter, with an int, with a double and with a String. Each prints a label, so that we can see which one runs.

slides.heading: Rules for overloading
slides.body_md: Overloaded constructors must differ in the **number**, the **types** or the **order** of their parameters. Different parameter **names** are not enough.

rows: `Pack(int a, double b)` and `Pack(double a, int b)`
the order of the types differs
only the names differ: constructor Pack(int) is already defined in class Pack

visual.alt: Table of overloading rules: constructors may differ in the types, the order or the number of parameters, but two constructors that differ only in parameter names are rejected by the compiler
visual.caption: Parameter names never distinguish overloaded constructors.

slides.narration: The compiler tells overloaded constructors apart only by their parameter lists. They may differ in the number of parameters, in their types, or in the order of the types. They may not differ only in the names of the parameters. Two constructors that each take one int, with different names, are duplicates, and the compiler reports an error.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which constructor runs?

visual.alt: Trace table of four calls of the overloaded constructors of Meter: the call with no argument prints no argument; the call with 5 prints int 5; the call with 5.0 prints double 5.0; the call with "5" prints String 5
visual.caption: The arguments of new decide which constructor runs.

slides.narration: Let us trace four creation statements. With no argument, the constructor without parameters runs and prints no argument. With the int five, the int constructor runs. With five point zero, which is a double, the double constructor runs. With the string five in quotes, the string constructor runs. The arguments of new decide which constructor is executed.

slides.heading: Matching the call with a constructor
slides.body_md: The compiler compares the **arguments** of the `new` statement with the **parameter lists** and picks the constructor that fits.

slides.heading: When there is no exact match
slides.body_md: If no constructor fits exactly, Java **widens** the argument: `char` to `int`, `int` to `long`, `long` to `float`, `float` to `double`. A constructor is chosen only if the widening works.

nodes.label: char to int to long to float to double
No match, or two equal matches: compile-time error

visual.alt: Flow of how Java chooses a constructor: look for an exact match, otherwise widen the arguments along char to int to long to float to double, and report a compile-time error if there is no match or two equally good matches
visual.caption: Choosing among overloaded constructors

slides.narration: What if no constructor fits exactly? Java widens the argument, step by step, along the chain char, int, long, float and double. It stops at the first type for which a constructor exists. If there is no such constructor, or if two constructors fit equally well, the compiler reports an error. Nothing is ever narrowed automatically.

A long argument is widened to double, so the double constructor runs and prints seven point zero. A float argument also widens to double, and prints two point five.

Passing an argument to a class that has only the default constructor fails. And an object cannot be passed where no constructor takes that class. Each message is the real one from the compiler.

So the messages follow the order of the new statements, not the order in which the constructors are written in the class. In the program the first gate uses the parameterised constructor, the second the default one, the third the parameterised one again. The summary line comes last.

slides.heading: Constructor against method
slides.body_md: A constructor and a method are both members of a class, but they differ in **name**, **return type**, **how they are executed** and **purpose**.

rows: as often as it is called
performs an action or a calculation
a default constructor if the class has none

visual.alt: Table of the differences between a constructor and a method: name, return type, how it is executed, number of times, purpose and what the compiler supplies

slides.narration: Now we compare constructors and methods. A constructor has the class name, while a method has any valid name. A constructor has no return type, while a method must have one. A constructor is executed automatically by new, once for each object, while a method runs only when it is called, as often as needed. A constructor initialises, a method does a task.

slides.heading: Seeing the difference in a run

visual.alt: Table of constructor against method calls: new alone prints constructor ran / 12; with two calls of setHour the output is constructor ran / method ran / method ran / 9, so the constructor ran once and the method twice
visual.caption: The constructor runs once; the method runs on every call.

slides.narration: The run shows the difference. Creating the clock prints constructor ran once, without any call. The two calls of the set hour method print method ran twice, because a method runs on every call. A constructor, on the other hand, cannot be called again through the object. The table also shows the compiler messages when someone tries.

sections.heading: 6. Constructor against method
sections.body_md:
| Constructor | Method |
|---|---|
| Same name as the class | Any valid name |
| No return type, not even void | A return type is compulsory (void if nothing is returned) |
| Executed automatically by new | Executed only when called |
| Executed once for each object | Executed as often as it is called |
| Initialises the data members | Performs an action or a calculation |
| Compiler supplies a default one if the class has none | Compiler supplies nothing |

sections.heading: 7. Writing a class with constructors in the exam
sections.body_md:
A 15-mark program usually asks for a class with **data members**, a **default constructor**, a **parameterised constructor** (often overloaded), a **compute** method and a **display** method, and a **main** that creates the objects.

1. Declare the data members.
2. Write the constructors: class name, no return type; use this when the parameters have the names of the data members.
3. Write compute (decisions, calculations) and display.
4. In main, read the input with Scanner, create each object with new and call its methods.
5. Add the variable description or comments.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing void (or any return type) before a constructor: it becomes a method that new never calls.
- Writing a constructor name that differs from the class name.
- Believing that Parcel p; runs the constructor.
- Calling new Parcel() when only a parameterised constructor exists.
- name = name; without this, so the data member keeps its default value.
- Overloading with constructors that differ only in parameter names.
- Trying to call a constructor through an object, p.Parcel().

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Definition: the meaning, and two characteristics (class name, no return type, automatic execution).
- Differences: one mark for each point stated for both.
- Output questions: each line in the exact order, with the constructor messages in the order of the new statements.
- Programs (15 marks): class and data members, each constructor, the compute method, objects created in main and output, variable description or comments.

questions.stem_md: Which description of a constructor in Java is correct?

options.text_md: A member method that must be called by the programmer once for every object, after the object is created
A member method with the same name as its class and no return type, executed automatically when an object is created
A data member that stores the number of objects of the class
A method of the Scanner class that reads the values of the data members

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A member method with the same name as its class and no return type, executed automatically when an object is created. A constructor is written inside the class, bears the class name, has no return type and is run by the new operator itself. Nothing has to call it, which rules out the description that needs a call from the programmer; it is also a method, not a data member, and it has no connection with Scanner.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Kite. The constructor has exactly the name of the class, including the capital letter, because Java is case-sensitive. The word new is an operator used to create the object, not a part of the constructor name.

questions.stem_md: A class is named Clock. Which of the following is a valid header of its constructor?

`void Clock()`
`int Clock()`
`static Clock()`

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** `Clock()`. A constructor has no return type at all, not even void. With void or int in front, the line declares an ordinary method that merely has the same name as the class. A static constructor is rejected by javac with "modifier static not allowed here".

questions.stem_md: At which moment is the constructor of a class executed?

options.text_md: When a reference variable of the class is declared
When the main method of the program ends
When an object of the class is created with the operator new
When any method of the object is called for the first time

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** When an object of the class is created with the operator new. Declaring a reference such as Parcel p; creates no object, so no constructor runs. The constructor runs as the new operator builds the object: in a real run, the declaration, a print statement and then the creation give `Declared / Parcel created / Created`.

questions.stem_md: What is the main use of a constructor?

To decide which method of the class is executed first

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** To initialise the data members of an object at the time of its creation. A constructor gives the data members of the new object their starting values. Memory is not released by a constructor, keyboard input is the work of Scanner, and the order of methods is decided by the statements written in main.

**Correct option: (a)** `3`. The default constructor runs once for every object that is created with new, so the three new expressions print the message three times. It does not run once per class, and it does not wait for a method call.

The statement p = new Parcel(); then builds the object, which runs the constructor and prints its message, and the last println follows.

**Assertion (A):** A constructor can be called again and again on the same object, for example p.Parcel(), to reset its data members.

**Reason (R):** A constructor is invoked automatically only once for an object, at the moment the object is created with new.
